extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, AI/automated-theorem-proving researchers, and readers interested in building human-like proof-finding systems
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and desiderata for designing or evaluating systems that find proofs in a way resembling human mathematicians (producing motivated, comprehensible, and practically useful proofs rather than merely formal certificates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully justified / motivated proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A ``fully justified proof'' is defined as “a proof together with convincing motivations for the steps.” (Alternative suggested terms: “motivated proof” or “explicitly motivated proof”.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include not just a validity check but also the convincing motivations for each step so the proof reads as a human-style argument. Avoid interpreting “justified” merely as formal correctness; the motivation (why steps are natural) must be part of the artifact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human vs Boring vs Mysterious proof classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition proofs into Human Mathematics (what humans can prove), Boring (junk proofs), and Mysterious (idea-free proofs that may be concise but incomprehensible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to guide target behavior: aim for Human Mathematics and avoid producing overwhelming amounts of Boring or Mysterious proofs. The comment suggests Mysterious proofs are numerous and that characterizing what makes Human proofs special (e.g. simplicity) is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical simplicity as hallmark of human proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Mathematical proofs may exhibit some kind of “radical simplicity” — a simplicity that makes them recognizable and attractive to humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for structural characterizations of simplicity that distinguish human-style proofs from idea-free certificates; such characterizations should be non-trivial and useful for limiting search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental images / mental playgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians use mental images described as an imagined place with simple assertions and operative rules (a “mental playground”), enabling quick constructions (e.g. drawing regions, zooming in, constructing lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design representations or symbolic analogues of these mental images (rules for what can be readily constructed or thought about) to let the prover mimic geometric/structural intuition. Examples discussed: proving R^2 is Hausdorff, constructing Venn diagrams, planarity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play with objects / domain familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Human problem-solving involves ‘play’ with objects to build intuition — e.g. playing with small integers leads to noticing patterns like proximity to powers of two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either provide the prover with fruits of such play (hand-coded hints or a database of useful facts) or enable it to learn/explore those facts itself; initial practical work may focus on encoding useful heuristics rather than full exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence / ergonomics of proofs (good proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project aims not merely to find proofs but to find proofs that are “eloquent and ergonomic” — proofs that are natural, readable, and satisfying to humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate outputs on aesthetics/readability in addition to correctness; such qualities may be prioritized even if the algorithm is slower than brute force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff between proof quality and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether a machine that gives a ‘good proof’ but with poor time complexity (e.g., exponential time) should still be regarded as a success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly consider time-vs-quality tradeoffs; define acceptable classes/functions f(n) where producing a good proof in o(f(n)) is viewed as valuable. Empirical thresholds and domain-dependent standards should be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ‘rabbit out of the hat’ proofs / immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Good proofs should avoid unexplained, magical-looking steps (the ‘rabbit out of the hat’ phenomenon) and instead exhibit immediacy and natural construction choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bias toward proofs that feel immediate or familiar (use canonical constructions, show why steps arise), and prefer proofs that provide motivating explanations for steps rather than surprising certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent geometric intuition symbolically
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be possible to represent human geometric intuition in a symbolic form that is less efficient than human thinking but still helpful to computers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop symbolic primitives or rules that capture aspects of geometric mental images (e.g. ability to construct regions, reason about inside/outside, directed cyclic orders around vertices) so provers can mimic diagrammatic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of diagrams / visualization for certain problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Some problems (e.g., 4-circle Venn diagram existence, planarity of K5) are much easier with diagrams; visualization seems essential for certain classes of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either equip provers with diagrammatic reasoning capabilities or create symbolic surrogates that capture the same insights; flag such problems as those requiring special representation modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term memory and cognitive constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Human mental images typically do not explicitly represent many items at once (there are short-term memory limits, e.g., 3–7 items), and larger structures are represented implicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model cognitive constraints in the prover (e.g., limited working-set at a time) and encourage strategies like noticing symmetry or patterns to reduce combinatorial explosion; consider notion of ‘images on paper’ vs ‘in head’ with differing stability/capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hints: formalization, recording, and comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Hints or built-in skills should be explicit, formally represented, and recorded so their effects can be compared across problems. (E.g. record hint-sets used during runs.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store exact hint-sets, parameters, and versions so experiments are reproducible; allow contributors to add alternative hints and test their empirical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of prover runs and database of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs and the runs that produced them should be reproducible: record exact inputs, hint-sets, parameters, and prover version, and store them in a browsable database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable reconstruction of prover runs (the ‘stories of finding’ proofs) at any detail level to support statistical study and evaluation of methods and hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of hints as human vs superhuman / notion of cheating
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a hint is considered ‘cheating’ or ‘human’ can be operationalized: a hint is ‘superhuman’ if it makes the system better than any humans on certain problems or if the usage stories don’t look natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess hints empirically: do they help many problems, only a few, slow down other problems, or make the system exceed human performance unnaturally? Use these measures rather than subjective complaints about cheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural properties of proofs enabling feasible search
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek structural properties of ‘fully justified proofs’ (not tautological definitions) whose presence makes proofs tractable to find by algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify non-trivial, objective structural constraints (e.g., types of motifs, bounded complexity of motivations) that can be used to restrict search while preserving interesting human-relevant proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conscious vs subconscious search processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Human idea-generation includes subconscious searches that produce seemingly unexplained ideas; these processes differ from the conscious search humans can report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling human-style search, consider mechanisms analogous to subconscious exploration (e.g., background stochastic search, candidate-generation pipelines) as well as explicit, reportable strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multiple proofs per theorem to analyze hint effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The proofs database should include multiple proofs of the same theorem that used different hint-sets so their comparative effects can be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store alternative proofs and their generation metadata to compare how different hints influence outcomes (coverage, speed, naturalness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hints granularity: formal expressions vs built-in modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Hints can be formal expressions or built-in skills (software modules); representing hints formally makes it easier to record, compare, and potentially learn them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer formalizable hint representations when feasible, so they can be logged, analyzed, and possibly learned; built-in modules are acceptable but should have clear interfaces and usage logs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-domain alignment and evaluation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be strategically useful to choose problem domains closer to the machine’s natural capabilities (e.g., discrete problems) for early successes and iterative progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing system performance, consider the match between the problem domain and the system’s strengths; benchmark on domains where human intuitions are less critical initially, then broaden scope.
